title: When to prototype in Figma and when to design in the browser
excerpt: Use Figma vs browser prototyping as a split: Figma for structure and options, the browser when type, motion, and real content decide the question.
alt: A hand holding a stylus over a tablet covered in wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside it. The sketches are for structure; the keyboard is for the moment the browser has to answer.
caption: Structure on the tablet, truth in the browser. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When is Figma the right place to decide?
faqs.answer: Use Figma while you are choosing structure: what the screen is for, how many steps exist, and which of two directions is worth building. Comparing options is cheap there. Stay in Figma when the open question is about layout and content order, and nobody is yet arguing about a font rendering or a transition.

faqs.question: When should we move into the browser?
faqs.answer: Move when the decision depends on real type, real words, motion, or the width of a phone. A prototype that fakes those things will answer a different question than the one you ship. Hanabi uses Figma for the options and production code for the decisions that only show up in the browser.

faqs.question: Do we have to throw away the Figma file after we start coding?
faqs.answer: Keep the file as the map of structure and as the place options were rejected. Update it when a browser decision changes the structure, so a drifted frame is not a second source of truth. The shipped interface is the authority, and the file should be brought back into line the same day.

markdown:
The choice in Figma vs browser prototyping is about what the decision depends on. Use Figma to settle structure and to compare options. Move to the browser when type, motion, or the real content would change the answer. Both tools belong on a Hanabi project. They are not rival religions. They answer different questions, and using the wrong one makes a confident decision about the wrong object.

A small team loses days by polishing a picture of a page that cannot survive contact with its own headline, or by coding three directions that could have been rejected in an afternoon of frames. The split below is a way to spend the day on the question you actually have.

## Figma while the question is structure

Structure is the set of regions, the order of decisions, and the path from one step to the next. While those are still open, a design file is the faster place. You can put two options side by side. You can throw one away without a pull request. You can talk about the job without also talking about a build error.

Use that phase to name the screen, the primary action, and what is deliberately missing. Wireframes are enough when the question is "do we need this step." High-fidelity frames are useful when the question is "can someone see the action," and even then they are a hypothesis. Write the real headline in the frame. Placeholder words hide overflow, and overflow is often the whole problem.

Keep the file legible for the next person. One page for the flow, one for the options you rejected, with a line on why. A file that is only the winner, with no trace of the rejected path, will relitigate the same argument next month. The rejected frame is part of the decision.

Figma is also the right place to agree the brand's type, color, and the few components you will repeat, before those decisions are rebuilt by hand in code. A founder can react to a type pair in a frame faster than they can react to a branch. Take the reaction. Then stop refining shadows. Shadows are rarely the question that needed the meeting.

## The browser when reality can change the call

Type renders differently in a browser than in a design tool. Line breaks change. A font that looked elegant at a large size may be hard to read at the size the phone actually uses. If the open question is whether the first sentence fits and can be read, answer it in the browser with the type you will ship.

Real content changes layout. The longest name in the database, the offer in the founder's actual words, a translation that runs longer: these break frames that were drawn around short examples. Put the difficult content in early. A prototype filled with even words is a prototype of a different product.

Motion is almost impossible to judge from a click-through of still frames. You can indicate that something moves. You cannot feel whether the movement explains a relationship or merely delays the read. Hanabi designs those moments in the browser, with the Motion library, on the real component. If the movement does not earn its place beside the words, it comes out. A frame with a note that says "animate this" is a reminder, not a decision.

The phone width belongs in the same category. A scaled-down artboard is a picture of a phone. A browser on a device is the phone. Check the thumb's path, the sticky header's cost, and the moment the keyboard covers a field. Those are not polish. They change what the first screen is.

## What production code is allowed to decide

Once a direction is chosen, building it is a design tool. React, TypeScript, and Tailwind are how Hanabi makes the choice durable. Components with real props show whether the empty state, the error, and the long name were imaginary. A prop that is awkward to pass is often a screen that is awkward to understand. Listen to that friction. It is information about the interface.

This does not mean you code every option. Code the survivor. If two ideas are still alive, you have not finished the Figma phase, or you are looking at a question only the browser can settle, in which case build the smallest slice that answers it. A throwaway route with the real type is enough. A full feature behind a flag, fully wired to the database, is too much for a question about a headline.

Keep the coded slice on a staging URL the founder can open without a designer's machine. Comments on a URL are comments on the product. Comments on a picture are comments on a picture. When the discussion is about whether to ship, the URL is the honest artifact.

The W3C's [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) are easier to take seriously in the browser, where you can tab through the page, read a name with a screen reader, and see whether focus is visible. The guidelines are a technical standard organized under perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust, and conformance means meeting success criteria. A Figma frame can plan for that. It cannot show you that focus is trapped in a menu. When the question is whether the page is operable, the browser is the prototype that counts. Do not treat a green annotation in the file as a completed check.

## A simple rule for the next task

Ask what would change your mind.

- If a different arrangement of regions would change your mind, stay in Figma and draw both.
- If the true headline, the true type, or a real device would change your mind, open the browser.
- If a transition's timing or a reduced-motion version would change your mind, build the motion on the component.
- If nothing in the browser could change your mind, you are polishing, and you should stop.

Write the question at the top of the task so the team does not "jump to code" or "stay in Figma" out of habit. Habit is expensive in both directions. Designers who refuse the browser ship surprises. Engineers who refuse the file build the first idea that compiles.

Update the file when the browser overturns a structural choice, so the next person does not revive the old frame as if it were current. The same day is the right time. A week later, nobody remembers which version won, and the argument returns.

## Motion is the usual reason to leave the frame

Still frames can imply a fade. They cannot tell you whether the fade helps someone understand that a panel came from a button, or whether it makes them wait. That judgment wants the real component, a slow version, and a version that barely moves for people who ask the system to reduce motion. The next piece stays on that judgment: [motion that helps, and motion that makes people leave](/blog/motion-that-helps).

When you want the structure and the production interface from the same team, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The studio uses Figma and the browser on purpose, and ships the answer that survives both.
